newsitem.title: USA: Near-term credit view cloudy for PC makers-experts.
newsitem.headline: Near-term credit view cloudy for PC makers-experts.

text.p: The near-term credit outlook for computer hardware manufacturers calls for overcast skies as companies adjust to escalating competition and a shift to more open systems technology, corporate debt analysts said.
The longer-term scenario, however, is bright as demand for new technology is expected to remain at lofty levels.
The apparent paradox, corporate pundits said, is almost a trademark of the industry.

Experts said the nature of the high-technology market itself, characterized by stiff price competition, short product life cycles and high investment requirements, makes firms more susceptible to earnings and cash flow volatility.
And nothing shakes corporate debt investors more than uncertainty about future revenues.

"The first question is: Why am I going to lend money to a company ... mainly if I don't know if that company is going to survive?," said Martin Fridson, high-yield market analyst at Merrill Lynch and Co Inc.

Analysts also said that, among other things, the recent growth of the Internet worldwide computer network has forced the industry to quickly move from proprietary to lower margin, more commodity-oriented open systems technology.
Analysts said such phenomena affect the high-technology sector in general, but hardware makers in particular.

"The same forces apply to hardware and software. But they're accentuated in hardware because the technology cycle is faster," said Molly Toll-Reed, director and high-tech analyst at credit rating agency Standard and Poor's.

"The need to roll out new products is accentuated in hardware ... You can't stop developing products in software either, but you don't have to be rolling out a new product line every nine months, like you do at hardware," she added.

Analysts said Apple Computer Inc, the Macintosh computer manufacturer, has become a clear-cut example of how abrupt shifts in the marketplace can deteriorate a firm's credit outlook and erode investor confidence.
"Apple had a proprietary system and the industry moved away from proprietary hardware platforms ... Apple didn't move on a timely basis," Toll-Reed said.

"They moved over the last year or so to try to license their system and open it up to broader usage ... but it's coming too late. Failure to adapt to industry changes kills anybody, including Apple," she added.
Apple entered the long-term corporate debt market in February 1994, when S&P granted the firm an A-minus rating.
Since then, the company was downgraded to BBB in August 1994, to BB-minus in January 1996 and to its current junk bond rating of B-plus with a negative outlook, following several quarters of losses.
"It just shows that if you're behind the curve in the technology wave, you can quickly get swamped," said Kingman Penniman, high-yield investment analyst at KDP Investment Advisors Inc.
Apple is not alone. Unisys Corp also shares the same B-plus rating from S&P with a negative outlook.
Analysts said the higher business risk profile of the technology sector forces companies to keep very conservative balance sheet structures and sizable cash balances.
Thus, they added, the ability to quickly shift direction and adopt new standards is seen as key for the companies to keep their heads above water.
"Past success does not guarantee future success in an industry in which annual growth rates sometimes exceed 50 percent," Toll-Reed said.
Besides, analysts at S&P estimate that after worldwide growth of 25 percent in 1995, global PC industry growth is expected to moderate to the high teens this year.
The U.S., which accounts for 40 percent of the worldwide market, led the slowdown in the first half of 1996.

However, the 14 and 12 percent growth rates experienced in the domestic PC industry in the first and second quarters, respectively, are very healthy by most standands, keeping most analysts bullish over the long term.
Due to the sector's volatility, most high tech hardware manufacturers that decided to issue debt ended up doing so in the speculative, high-yield market.

A close look at S&P's credit ratings chart shows that eight of the 11 covered companies have been granted a "stable" outlook, including giants like International Business Machines and Hewlett-Packard Corp.
Two firms have negative outlooks, while only one has captured S&P's heart and received a positive outlook rating -- Dell Computer Corp, a consumer-direct PC vendor.

"Sucessful companies will continue to evaluate -- and change, if needed -- their cultures, cost structures, product lines, response time and marketing focus to effectively implement their business strategies," Toll-Reed said.
